clue.text: Plain and honest speaker, unlike Beckham famously?

definitions.meaning: someone who says things directly and truthfully
David Beckham was famous for bending free kicks (the film 'Bend It Like Beckham'), so a player who shoots without curl is the opposite

explanation.surface: A frank talker is contrasted with a footballer known for curling the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is literal: one who shoots straight, whereas Beckham bent his shots.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who speaks candidly and without evasion is idiomatically called this.

clue.text: Careless Whisper coming from faulty speaker?

definitions.text: Careless Whisper coming from faulty speaker?

parts.words: Careless Whisper coming from faulty speaker?
parts.note: read the song title literally: a careless utterance escaping from a speaker who makes an error

explanation.surface: George Michael's hit song 'Careless Whisper' crackles out of a broken loudspeaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Careless Whisper' looks like the song title and 'speaker' like audio equipment; read instead as an unguarded remark from a person talking.
explanation.definitionFit: An inadvertent verbal error made while talking is an idiomatic phrase for such a careless utterance.

clue.text: He played Superman, note, whom film was all about

parts.note: re is a note of the sol-fa scale
the 1950 film 'All About Eve' was all about Eve

explanation.surface: A trivia question about the actor who played Superman and a film's subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Reeve was the actor who starred as the Man of Steel in the 1978 film.

clue.text: Close to Sgt Bilko, worried about new part of psychology test

indicators.note: worried suggests letters being agitated and turned about into a new order
the close of a word is its final letter, here taken from Sgt

explanation.surface: Sergeant Bilko, the TV con-man, frets about some new test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried about' rearranges BILKO with N; 'Close to' gives the T of Sgt, set at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rorschach test shows a subject ambiguous ink shapes to interpret, so each card is one element of it.

clue.text: Time to take small teaspoonful for one kind of rash?

indicators.note: one word taking another in means it holds it inside

parts.note: an hour is a unit of time
tsp is the short form of teaspoon(ful) in recipes

explanation.surface: A medical tip: wait a while and take a little teaspoon of medicine for a skin rash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rash' is not a skin complaint but the adjective: Harry Hotspur, Shakespeare's impetuous knight, is the rash type.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotspur was the nickname of the impulsive Henry Percy, so the word names a headstrong, reckless person.

clue.text: Almost certain to go unnoticed in tower above

indicators.note: almost means the word falls one letter short of complete, losing its end

parts.note: certain means sure
to pass is to go by without being remarked upon

explanation.surface: Someone almost sure to slip by unseen in a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the last letter of SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: To exceed or outdo something is to tower above it figuratively.

clue.text: Old British minister to spy

parts.note: to minister to someone is to serve them

explanation.surface: A former British government minister turns out to be a spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minister' looks like a noun (a politician) but 'minister to' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To spy something is to catch sight of it, which is to notice or watch it.

clue.text: Journalist supporting top space traveller Armstrong did this

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece supporting others sits beneath them

parts.note: to top is to trump, to beat
ET is the film's extraterrestrial
ED, an editor, is the stock crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter backing a top astronaut, Neil Armstrong, on his achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'space traveller' pushes toward Neil Armstrong; the definition means jazz trumpeter Louis Armstrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Armstrong was a celebrated jazz horn player, so he blew a brass instrument for a living.

clue.text: Busy surgeries tend to accommodate occasionally weary health worker

indicators.note: to accommodate is to take in and house, so one piece goes inside
busy suggests letters bustling about into a new order
occasionally means only some letters are taken, at regular intervals

explanation.surface: Busy GP surgeries tend to take in tired patients now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy' rearranges SURGERIES TEND; 'occasionally' picks E and R from weary, and 'to accommodate' sets ER inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A qualified nurse registered with the professional body is a medical professional caring for patients.

clue.text: Curry? Use some spices Kate roasted

indicators.note: to use some of something is to take only part of it, so a run of letters is lifted from the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Cooking advice: use some of the spices Kate roasted in a curry.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'Curry? Use' wrongly took in 'Use'; the definition is 'Curry?' alone, with 'Use some' the hiding signal. 'Curry' is John Curry, not the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: John Curry was the British Olympic figure-skating champion of 1976, an example of a skater.

clue.text: Cast of The Last of Us needing breather

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, here from Us

parts.note: a lung is the organ one breathes with

explanation.surface: The actors of the TV series 'The Last of Us' need a breather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like a noun for actors; it is the past tense of the verb, meaning thrown.
explanation.definitionFit: To have thrown or hurled something is to have flung it, a past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Have something in common, done with drink

parts.note: something done is over, finished
to lap is to drink as a cat does

explanation.surface: Two people share an interest, and then they're finished with their drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that partly coincide or share ground are said to coincide in part this way.

clue.text: Ace rugby player, outstanding at the back, and fit

indicators.note: at the back places this piece last in the answer

parts.note: A is the card abbreviation for ace
a prop is a front-row forward in rugby
O/S is the accounting abbreviation for outstanding, owed

explanation.surface: A star rugby forward, brilliant in defence and in top physical shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding' and 'fit' look like praise for the player; one is O/S, the other the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something opportune or relevant to the matter at hand is suitable, appropriate.

clue.text: Successes as United start to press Son

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for United in team names

indicators.note: the start to a word is its first letter, here of press

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son in genealogies

explanation.surface: A football report: United succeed as Son (Heung-min) starts to press.
explanation.walkthrough: Son looks like the Korean footballer Son Heung-min; it is just S.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'ups and downs', good times or highs are the plural of a fortunate turn.

clue.text: Dorothy was sucked in by this con artist

definitions.text: Dorothy was sucked in by this
definitions.meaning: in The Wizard of Oz Dorothy is carried off by a tornado
a swindler who twists the truth

explanation.surface: Dorothy from Oz was fooled by a trickster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sucked in' reads as 'fooled', but it is literal: the tornado lifted her house.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is colloquially called by this name in the US, and a cheat or fraudster also bears it.

clue.text: Popular poem cut short by worker, uncouth

parts.note: in means popular, fashionable

indicators.note: cut short means the word loses its end letter

parts.note: an elegy is a mournful poem
the worker ant is the stock crossword worker

explanation.surface: A popular poem is curtailed by a crude labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' drops the Y of ELEGY.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking grace or refinement, clumsy and unpolished, is the sense shared by both words.

clue.text: Slippery sort, somewhat unfeeling

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A slippery character who is rather cold-hearted.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is a slimy fish, hard to hold, and figuratively an evasive person.

clue.text: Respect rocking Rod!

indicators.note: rocking shakes the letters about into a new order

explanation.surface: A fan cheers singer Rod Stewart's rendition of 'Respect'.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod reads as Rod Stewart; it is a ceremonial staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's ornamental staff of office is a kind of rod.

clue.text: Firm with bully

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A company accused of complicity with a bully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bully' is the verb: to cow someone is to intimidate them.
explanation.definitionFit: To intimidate someone into submission is to cow them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Picked up pearly queen's cocktail to examine closely

indicators.note: picked up means heard, so the word is taken as said aloud

parts.note: a highball is a long cocktail; a pearly queen is a Cockney figure, and Cockneys drop the H, giving 'ighball

explanation.surface: A Cockney pearly queen's drink is overheard while someone looks hard at it.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearly kings and queens are London Cockney charity figures in pearl-button costumes; Cockney speech drops the H, so 'ighball' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare at intently, scrutinising someone, is an informal verb built from the organ of sight.

clue.text: Leave what one wearing 24 has?

definitions.meaning: 24 is OBI, a sash, so its wearer has a band on

explanation.surface: A question about leaving and what someone in a sash wears.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into three words: a wearer of the sash at 24 across has a band on.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert or forsake somewhere is to leave it for good.

clue.text: A butcher's can get wrapping rump of steak

indicators.note: wrapping means the outer pieces enclose another

parts.note: can is slang for a lavatory, a loo
to get something is to see, understand it

indicators.note: the rump is the hind end, so the final letter of steak

explanation.surface: A butcher's shop selling rump steak wrapped up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A butcher's' is Cockney rhyming slang: butcher's hook = look; it is the definition, not a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang 'have a butcher's' means take a quick glance, the same as an informal quick inspection.

clue.text: Rogue sealing heartless deal in scam

indicators.note: sealing means enclosing, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: a swine is a contemptible rogue

indicators.note: heartless removes the middle, leaving only the outer letters

explanation.surface: A rogue closing a crooked deal as part of a fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: A con or fraud to cheat people of money is a scam.

clue.text: Wind from South Island with legendary bird beginning to circle round

parts.note: the roc is a giant bird of Arabian legend

indicators.note: the beginning to a word is its first letter, here of circle

parts.note: O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A wind blows from New Zealand's South Island as a mythical bird begins to circle.
explanation.walkthrough: South Island looks like New Zealand's; it is S and I.
explanation.definitionFit: The hot dusty wind blowing from North Africa across the Mediterranean is the sirocco.

clue.text: A slice from Hoddle, if nicely set up towards the box?

indicators.note: set up in a down clue means the letters are read upward, backwards
a slice is just part, so a run of letters is taken from these words

explanation.surface: Glenn Hoddle, England footballer, slices a nicely set-up shot toward the penalty box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slice' and 'set up' sound like football; they signal taking DLEIFNI from the words and reversing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverbially, it means into the central area of a field, away from the boundary, i.e. toward the middle.

clue.text: Sash in Bilbao, with alb braided all around

indicators.note: braided suggests strands woven together, so these letters are mixed together all around

explanation.surface: A sash seen in Bilbao, worn with a priest's alb with braiding all round it.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus ALB shuffles to BILBAO.
explanation.definitionFit: An obi is the broad sash worn around a Japanese kimono.

clue.text: Herb for cooking free range ducks outside

indicators.note: one piece sits outside the other, enclosing it

parts.note: a duck is zero, O, in cricket; two give OO

indicators.note: free lets the letters loose into a new order

explanation.surface: Seasoning free-range ducks before cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free range' looks like a farming term; 'free' rearranges RANGE, held by OO.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is an aromatic plant whose leaves are used to season food, an example of a culinary herb.

clue.text: Collar Scotsman, hooligan …

parts.note: a ruff is a frilled Elizabethan collar
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: Collaring a Scottish troublemaker; the ellipsis runs on to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent, lawless person is a thug or ruffian.

clue.text: Country inn Admiral regularly visited

indicators.note: regularly visited means letters are taken at even intervals, every other one

explanation.surface: An admiral regularly visited a country inn.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a nation in South Asia.

clue.text: … smashing piano

explanation.surface: Continuing the hooligan: he is smashing a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis paints a hooligan smashing a piano; both words are definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A full-size concert piano is called a grand, and 'grand' is also slang for excellent.

clue.text: Winner dispatching ball casually: score, deuce

indicators.note: casually suggests a careless, jumbled order
dispatching means sending away, so letters are removed

parts.note: a ball is round, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A tennis match: a player serves casually at deuce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispatching' removes O from SCORE; 'casually' rearranges SCRE with DEUCE.
explanation.definitionFit: One who succeeds is a winner, someone who achieves success.

clue.text: Friendly relationship? It centred on brewing English beer bottles

indicators.note: bottles means holds inside, as a bottle holds its contents

parts.note: ale is a type of beer

indicators.note: brewing suggests ingredients mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: An English beer that holds the centre of a brewing friendship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewing' rearranges IT CENTRED ON, and 'bottles' sets the result between E and ALE.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1904 Anglo-French agreement's name became the term for any cordial understanding between nations.
